chapterTitle: Troubleshooting Load Balancer Connectivity and Performance Issues
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute live troubleshooting video. Start by showing a "503 Service Unavailable" error in a browser, and then immediately jump to the ALB's target group to show an unhealthy instance. Demonstrate how to SSH into the instance and stop the web server (e.g., Nginx) to simulate the issue. Then, walk through diagnosing with CloudWatch metrics, highlighting `UnHealthyHostCount` and `HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count` spikes. Next, show how to check the target's health status details for specific error messages. Demonstrate fixing the issue by restarting Nginx and observing the health status return to normal. Conclude with a visual checklist of common troubleshooting steps (CloudWatch, Access Logs, Security Groups, NACLs, App Logs) and a quick interactive quiz on interpreting 5xx errors.

---

screens.title: Troubleshooting Load Balancer Connectivity and Performance Issues
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build a repeatable troubleshooting habit for Application and Network Load Balancers. You will learn how to translate symptoms — like 5xx spikes, 503 responses, or slow requests — into focused checks using CloudWatch, access logs, health checks, and network diagnostics. I’ll show concrete signals to watch for, how to validate target group health, and how to rule out common network misconfigurations such as security group mismatches and NACL blocks. We’ll also walk through a short hands-on scenario where a stopped web server causes a “No Healthy Targets” state and a 503 error, and then verify recovery once the service is restored. By the end you’ll have a clear checklist: identify symptoms, confirm health checks, inspect metrics, drill into logs, validate network rules, and test connectivity. This approach reduces guesswork and helps you escalate only when the evidence shows it’s an application, configuration, or infrastructure problem. As you follow the screens, notice how monitoring, logs, and small connectivity tests work together to pinpoint the root cause.

keyIdea.title: Toolchain
keyIdea.text: CloudWatch + access logs + health checks + network checks form the diagnostic toolchain to isolate LB vs backend vs network faults.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.9 › Skills & Tools
Learning Objectives — Skills & Tools
Understand which metrics and logs to query, and how they map to root causes.
CloudWatch mapping
  • HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count → load balancer level issues such as no healthy targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count → backend application errors; inspect application logs.
  • HealthyHostCount / UnHealthyHostCount → health check failures driving routing problems.
Logs & network checks
  • Access logs provide per-request traceability; use Athena for queries.
  • VPC Flow Logs reveal blocked IP traffic caused by SG or NACL rules.
  • TargetConnectionErrorCount indicates connection setup failures between LB and targets.

screens.title: Identifying Symptoms
screens.narratorSegment: The first diagnostic move is to clearly identify the symptom. That means listening to user reports and translating them into measurable signals: are users seeing 5xx server errors, 4xx client errors, 503 service unavailable, 504 timeouts, or simply slow responses? Each class points to a different area. A spike in 5xx codes can mean the load balancer could not reach healthy targets or the targets are returning errors. A dominant Client 4xx pattern usually indicates client-side issues or misrouted requests. A 503 with “No Healthy Targets” is a direct pointer to health check failures. Slow responses and high latency often indicate overloaded targets or network congestion rather than immediate configuration errors. Concrete example: if several users report 503 and CloudWatch shows UnHealthyHostCount increased, you should immediately check the target group's health status and the instance’s service. A common misconception is to restart the load balancer first; instead, verify whether targets are unhealthy and why. Key takeaway: use the symptom to choose the right next tool — metrics, logs, or network checks — so you don’t waste time chasing unlikely causes. Ask yourself: does the data point to the load balancer, the network, or the application?

keyIdea.title: Symptom-driven triage
keyIdea.text: Classify errors (4xx/5xx/503/504/latency) to direct your next diagnostic tool and quickly narrow the fault domain.

content.html:
Core Concept
Identifying Symptoms
Translate user reports into diagnostic signals that guide investigation.
Common signals: 5xx spikes, 503, 504, high latency, unreachable app.
Interpretation: 503 + No Healthy Targets → health checks or SG/NACL issues.
Misconception: Restarting LB before checking targets wastes time; targets often cause 503s.
Key Takeaway

Symptoms determine the first checks: choose metrics for high-level signals, access logs for per-request detail, and health checks for immediate routing problems.

Symptom classification panel
5xx spike
Likely LB or backend errors. Check HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count and HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count.
503 / No healthy targets
Check target group health, service running, SG/NACL rules, and health check path/port.
504 Gateway Timeout
Likely the target didn’t respond before the idle timeout; examine idle timeout and target response times.
High latency
Indicates overloaded targets, network congestion, or slow application queries.
Example scenario
If users report 503 and UnHealthyHostCount increases in CloudWatch, go to the target group and inspect instance health details. That evidence avoids fruitless LB changes.

screens.title: CloudWatch Metrics for ALBs
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch is the first stop for aggregated signals. For Application Load Balancers the most diagnostic metrics are HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count, HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, HealthyHostCount and UnHealthyHostCount, TargetConnectionErrorCount, Latency, and ClientTLSNegotiationErrorCount for HTTPS listeners. Use these values together instead of reading a single metric in isolation. For example, a large HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count spike paired with UnHealthyHostCount > 0 strongly suggests the ALB is returning errors because it lacks healthy targets. By contrast, if HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count is high but HealthyHostCount is stable, the back end is likely returning 5xx responses and you should inspect application logs. TargetConnectionErrorCount indicates failures establishing connections between ALB and targets and often points to security group or NACL rules or resource exhaustion on the target. Latency helps you distinguish between connectivity errors and slow application responses. A common error is to treat Latency spikes as transient client problems; instead check target C P U, memory, or thread pools. A quick example: you see high TargetConnectionErrorCount and connection resets — verify that the target’s security group permits inbound from the ALB security group and that the instance is responsive on the health-check port. Closing question: which two metrics will you check first when you see a 5xx spike?

keyIdea.title: ALB metrics map
keyIdea.text: Correlate ELB-level and target-level metrics: matching spikes and health counts points to LB vs backend causes.

content.html:
Process
CloudWatch Metrics for ALBs
Use grouped metrics to pinpoint whether the load balancer or targets are the source of errors.
HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count — errors from the ALB itself, often no healthy targets.
HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count — backend application errors; check application logs and resource usage.
TargetConnectionErrorCount — connection failures between ALB and targets; check SGs and NACLs.
HealthyHostCount / UnHealthyHostCount — fast indicator whether targets pass health checks.
Concrete example
If HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count spikes and UnHealthyHostCount increases, check the target group. If the target returns 502 on health checks, inspect the service and its logs.
Quick metric comparison
When ELB metric up
Suspect load balancer-level issue or zero healthy targets.
When Target metric up
Suspect backend application errors or resource exhaustion.
High Latency
Investigate target performance, threads, DB calls, or network congestion.
TLS negotiation errors
For HTTPS, ClientTLSNegotiationErrorCount shows handshake problems between client and ALB.
Pro-tip
Always correlate at least two metrics before changing infrastructure: a single spike rarely tells the full story.

screens.title: CloudWatch Metrics for NLBs
screens.narratorSegment: Network Load Balancers operate at Layer 4 and provide a different set of signals. Key metrics include HealthyHostCount and UnHealthyHostCount, TargetConnectionErrorCount, TCP_Target_Reset_Count, UDP_Target_Dropped_Count, and ConsumedLCUs. These metrics reveal whether connections are being established and maintained, and whether the targets are dropping or resetting connections. For instance, a growing TCP_Target_Reset_Count often indicates the target is actively refusing or resetting connections — possibly due to the application closing sockets or resource constraints. Similarly, UDP_Target_Dropped_Count points to packet-level loss or unhandled port traffic. ConsumedLCUs helps you understand NLB capacity costs but can also indicate heavy load patterns. A common diagnostic step is to verify that the target’s security group and network ACLs allow the correct IP ranges and ephemeral ports to respond. One misconception is treating NLB behavior like ALB behavior: NLB preserves source IPs and connection errors often manifest differently. Practical check: if TargetConnectionErrorCount increases while HealthyHostCount drops, verify that the instance is listening and that network rules permit the connection and return traffic. How would you confirm whether resets are application-initiated or network-blocked? CloudWatch Metrics for NLBs means nlb metrics focus on connection-level behavior; resets and dropped counts point to target or network-level problems rather than http semantics.. In practical terms, layer 4 signals, connection errors, and consumed lcus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NLB signals
keyIdea.text: NLB metrics focus on connection-level behavior; resets and dropped counts point to target or network-level problems rather than HTTP semantics.

content.html:
Process
CloudWatch Metrics for NLBs
NLB metrics show connection-level behaviors and help narrow network vs target faults.
TCP_Target_Reset_Count — indicates connections reset by the target or network device.
UDP_Target_Dropped_Count — packets dropped by the target or not processed.
TargetConnectionErrorCount — failures establishing TCP connections from NLB to targets.
ConsumedLCUs — capacity metric; spikes can indicate traffic surges or scaling needs.
Practical check
If TCP resets increase, validate the target's listener process, OS socket limits, and security group rules allowing response ports. Remember NLB preserves client IPs, so target SG rules must account for client source addresses or VPC CIDR patterns.
Checklist
  • Confirm target process listening on correct port and binding to correct interface.
  • Check security group inbound rules for client IP ranges or VPC CIDR if source preservation applies.
  • Review Network ACLs on target subnets for both inbound and outbound ephemeral port rules.
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs for packet-level confirmation of blocked traffic.

screens.title: Analyzing Access Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Access logs provide the per-request detail that aggregated metrics cannot. ALB access logs record client IP, request timestamp, the ALB and target response codes, request processing time, target IP, and X-Forwarded-For headers. NLB access logs capture TCP/UDP connection records including source/destination IPs and ports and connection status. These logs are stored in S3 and are best queried with a service like Amazon Athena. A concrete example: when you see repeated 503 responses from an ALB, query the access logs for elb_status_code and target_status_code to see whether the ALB or the target returned the error and to identify problematic client IPs or request paths. A frequent mistake is to assume access logs are optional; in complex or intermittent issues per-request logs are essential for reproduction and root cause. When using Athena, parse timestamps and filter by load balancer name and target IP to narrow results to a window where a metric spike occurred. Final thought: always correlate access-log evidence with CloudWatch spikes and health-check timestamps to build a convincing chain of cause and effect. Analyzing Access Logs means access logs give the per-request evidence to confirm whether errors are generated by alb, nlb, or targets and to identify offending requests or clients.. In practical terms, using alb and nlb logs to find request-level causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Log granularity
keyIdea.text: Access logs give the per-request evidence to confirm whether errors are generated by ALB, NLB, or targets and to identify offending requests or clients.

content.html:
Definition
Analyzing Access Logs
Use access logs for per-request visibility and to correlate timestamps and response codes with CloudWatch metrics.
ALB logs: client IP, request time, elb_status_code, target_status_code, request processing time.
NLB logs: connection status, source/destination IP and ports, bytes transferred.
Athena query example
SELECT elb_status_code, target_status_code, count(*) as cnt
FROM alb_logs
WHERE load_balancer = 'cohortia-web-alb' AND date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY elb_status_code, target_status_code
ORDER BY cnt DESC;
Investigation tips
  • Filter logs to the metric spike window for precise correlation.
  • Look for client IPs generating many errors to detect abuse or misconfiguration.
  • Compare elb_status_code and target_status_code to locate the origin of the error.
Common mistake
Relying only on aggregated metrics can miss per-request anomalies and intermittent failures visible only in the access logs.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Target Group Health Check Failures
screens.narratorSegment: Health check failures are among the most common reasons for routing problems and 503 responses. Use a focused sequence: first, confirm the EC2 instance is running and the application process is listening on the expected port. For HTTP/HTTPS health checks, verify the configured path returns a 200 OK and that any authentication or application-layer redirects are not interfering. Next, confirm security groups allow inbound traffic on the health check port from the load balancer’s security group for ALBs or from the NLB private IPs/VPC CIDR range for NLBs. Check Network ACLs on the target subnet to ensure both inbound and outbound traffic on the health-check and ephemeral ports are allowed; remember NACLs are stateless so you must permit return traffic explicitly. Common application causes include the service being stopped, misconfigured binding addresses, or application logic returning errors. A frequent misconception is to alter health check thresholds before confirming the root cause; prefer fixing the underlying issue, then adjust thresholds if required for expected behavior. Example: if health checks report HTTP 502, inspect application logs to find errors generating the 502, restart the app only after you understand the error, then re-evaluate health checks. This sequence prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary configuration changes.

keyIdea.title: Health check triage
keyIdea.text: Systematically verify instance state, service listening, health path response, SG and NACL rules, and application logic before changing health check settings.

content.html:
Process Flow
Troubleshooting Target Group Health Check Failures
Follow these steps to find why targets are marked unhealthy.
Step-by-step checks
  1. Verify EC2 instance is running and reachable on the health-check port.
  2. Confirm the application process (Nginx, Apache, Node) is listening on the configured port and path.
  3. Check the target group's health check path and protocol actually return 200 OK.
  4. Verify security group rules: allow inbound health checks from the load balancer source.
  5. Inspect Network ACLs on the subnet for both inbound and outbound allow rules.
  6. Review application logs for errors causing failed responses.
Check your understanding
If health checks return connection refused, what two network elements should you verify before restarting the load balancer?
Example
Health checks fail with HTTP 502. Inspect application logs, find a misconfigured upstream, correct it, and watch the target return to healthy. Avoid changing health check path until you confirm the correct endpoint behavior.
Common mistake
Allowing only inbound NACL rules and forgetting to permit outbound ephemeral ports, which blocks return traffic and causes failed checks.

screens.title: Diagnosing Network Path Issues
screens.narratorSegment: A large class of load balancer problems stem from the network path. Start by validating the load balancer’s security group allows inbound traffic on listener ports from the expected client ranges. For ALBs, ensure the target’s security group allows traffic from the ALB’s security group; for NLBs, consider preserved source IPs and allow the appropriate client or VPC CIDR ranges. Check Network ACLs on both the load balancer and target subnets for explicit denies and remember that NACLs are stateless — you must allow both inbound and outbound flows. Confirm routing tables direct traffic correctly for internet-facing versus internal load balancers. If DNS resolution is used, verify the ALB DNS name resolves and that cached or stale DNS entries are not pointing to old resources. When in doubt, enable VPC Flow Logs on the affected subnets to record IP traffic and confirm whether packets are arriving and being dropped. A common misconception is that security groups are stateful enough to ignore NACLs; ignoring NACLs can leave packets dropped silently. Example diagnostic: if VPC Flow Logs show no accept entries from the load balancer to the target, inspect NACLs and routing immediately. The bottom line: verify all layers of the path — listeners, SGs, NACLs, routes, DNS, and flow logs — before concluding the application is at fault.

The bottom line: verify all layers of the path — listeners, SGs, NACLs, routes, DNS, and flow logs — before concluding the application is at fault.

keyIdea.title: Network path checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm listener ports, security group relationships, NACL allow rules both directions, route tables, and use VPC Flow Logs to find dropped traffic.

content.html:
Architecture
Diagnosing Network Path Issues
Walk the full network path from client to load balancer to target.
Security groups: ALB must allow listener ports; targets must allow from ALB SG or appropriate IP ranges.
Network ACLs: allow inbound and outbound on health and ephemeral ports; stateless rules require both directions.
Route tables: ensure internet-facing LBs have correct internet gateway routes; internal LBs route to target subnets.
DNS & connectivity: verify DNS resolves and test direct IP connectivity for NLBs with static IPs.
Use VPC Flow Logs
Enable Flow Logs to capture accept or reject entries for traffic between LB and targets. This is often decisive when SGs and NACLs disagree.
Diagnostic checklist
  • Confirm LB listeners open to client ranges.
  • Confirm target SG allows LB source (ALB SG or NLB IP/VPC CIDR).
  • Confirm NACL inbound/outbound for health and ephemeral ports.
  • Check route tables and DNS resolution.
  • Enable VPC Flow Logs and inspect accept/deny patterns.

screens.title: Systematic Troubleshooting Approach
screens.narratorSegment: When the issue is not obvious, follow a reproducible approach: verify symptoms, check health checks, review CloudWatch metrics, examine access logs, inspect network configuration, test connectivity, and finally review application logs. Start by clearly documenting what is failing and when. Then, check target group health — an unhealthy target frequently explains routing failures. Use CloudWatch to find metric anomalies that match the symptom window. Drill into access logs next to see per-request evidence and client patterns. After that, inspect security groups, NACLs, and route tables; enable VPC Flow Logs if you need packet-level confirmation. Perform connectivity checks with curl, telnet, or netcat from an instance in the same VPC, and from the target subnet to confirm reachability. Only after all network checks are clean should you dig into application logs. A common pitfall is interleaving configuration changes without locking in the evidence; always capture metrics and logs before and after changes so you can verify the effect. Example workflow: document 503 occurrence, confirm UnHealthyHostCount, query access logs for 503 timestamps, validate SG/NACLs and routes, run curl to the target health path, then examine application logs. This repeatable method helps you escalate with confidence when you need peer or vendor support.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable workflow
keyIdea.text: Follow a fixed sequence from symptoms to verification so you gather the right evidence and avoid unnecessary changes.

content.html:
Process
Systematic Troubleshooting Approach
1. Verify symptoms and timeframe.
2. Check health checks and target states.
3. Review CloudWatch metrics for anomalies.
4. Query access logs for per-request evidence.
5. Inspect SGs, NACLs, and routes.
6. Test connectivity with curl/telnet/netcat.
7. Check application logs last and verify fixes.
Pro-tip
Capture metrics and logs before making changes so you can validate whether your actions resolved the issue.
Example checklist
  1. Document symptom, affected LB and TG names, and the exact timestamps.
  2. Check UnHealthyHostCount and HTTPCode_* metrics during that window.
  3. Query access logs for matching timestamps and request paths.
  4. Run curl from an EC2 in the same VPC to the target health path.
  5. Fix application or security rules and re-observe metrics and health status.

screens.title: Hands-on: Simulate and Diagnose a No Healthy Targets Issue
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario walks you through a common lab: a stopped web service leading to an ALB reporting no healthy targets and users seeing 503 errors. First, SSH into the target instance and stop the web service to simulate the failure. Then observe CloudWatch for UnHealthyHostCount and HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count spikes. Next, inspect the target group in the console to confirm the instance health shows Unhealthy and view the health status details — it typically reports connection refused or a failed HTTP code. After diagnosing, restart the service and verify the instance returns to Healthy after a few successful health checks, and confirm the ALB returns traffic normally. A common misconception is to wait for too long before checking access logs; immediately capture logs and metrics so you can link timestamps. This exercise trains you to use the right tests: service state, health check response, CloudWatch, and access logs to confirm both failure and recovery. After the lab, reflect: did the evidence point to an application service failure, security configuration, or network problem? Hands-on: Simulate and Diagnose a No Healthy Targets Issue means simulated failure proves the workflow: induce symptom, observe metrics/logs, fix the service, verify health and metrics return to normal.. In practical terms, stop a web server, watch metrics, and verify recovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Simulated failure proves the workflow: induce symptom, observe metrics/logs, fix the service, verify health and metrics return to normal.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Simulate and Diagnose a No Healthy Targets Issue
Perform the following steps to reproduce and resolve a target health failure.
Step commands
# SSH into instance
ssh ec2-user@

# Stop web server to simulate failure
sudo systemctl stop nginx

# Check service status
sudo systemctl status nginx

# From another EC2 in VPC, test health check path
curl -v http:///:80/health

# Restart service to recover
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
After stopping the service, open CloudWatch and select ApplicationELB metrics for your load balancer. Observe UnHealthyHostCount and HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count for spikes. Then check the target group's Targets tab to see the Unhealthy state and the health status details. Restart the application and confirm the instance becomes Healthy and 5xx counts return to normal.
Checklist & tips
  • Capture timestamps before and after inducing the failure for log correlation.
  • Use an EC2 inside the same VPC for curl tests to avoid internet path differences.
  • Watch the health check interval and threshold values to estimate recovery delay.

screens.title: Testing Connectivity and Verifying Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: After you make a change — whether restarting a service, updating an SG, or changing a route — you must verify the fix. Begin by re-running the symptom checks and validating that CloudWatch metrics moved back toward expected levels. Use targeted connectivity tests: curl the health-check path and application endpoints from an EC2 in the same VPC and from the load balancer where possible. For TCP issues use telnet or netcat to confirm the port accepts connections. If you changed security groups, re-check VPC Flow Logs to see that previously dropped packets are now accepted. Observe the target group's health for successful status transitions; remember health checks often require a few intervals to flip state. Also re-query access logs for the same timestamps to confirm the request returned a successful code. A common error is to declare success based solely on the service process appearing 'running' — always confirm that traffic actually flows through the load balancer and the client sees a healthy response. Final question: after a fix, which two data sources will you compare to confirm recovery and why?

keyIdea.title: Verification
keyIdea.text: Always validate fixes by confirming health checks, CloudWatch metric recovery, connectivity tests, and access-log evidence of successful requests.

content.html:
Check Your Understanding
Testing Connectivity and Verifying Fixes
Use concrete tests and log evidence to confirm a fix worked as expected.
Connectivity tests: curl, telnet, nc from EC2 in same VPC and load balancer subnet.
Metric verification: confirm UnHealthyHostCount and 5xx counts return to baseline.
Log confirmation: query access logs for successful response codes at the expected timestamps.
Flow logs: ensure accept entries replace previously denied traffic after SG/NACL changes.
Final tip
Document the change, timestamp it, and capture before-and-after metrics so you can roll back if the fix had unexpected impact.
Quick verification checklist
  • Health check shows Healthy.
  • CloudWatch 5xx and UnHealthyHostCount returned to baseline.
  • Access logs show successful responses for the same requests.
  • VPC Flow Logs show accepted traffic if you modified network rules.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Experienced teams often run into a predictable set of mistakes. Security group mismatches are the most frequent cause of 'no healthy targets' or connection errors; ensure the target SG allows inbound from the load balancer source rather than broadly opening ports. Incorrect health check path or port is another common error: verify the configured path returns the expected 200 OK and that the application is actually listening on that port. Idle timeout settings can cause 504 Gateway Timeout errors when backend requests legitimately take longer than the default ALB idle timeout. DNS caching can mislead you into troubleshooting the wrong endpoint; clear caches or validate resolution before changing infrastructure. Target overload and resource exhaustion can masquerade as networking problems; always check application logs and resource metrics. One misconception is to immediately increase timeouts or change thresholds — this may hide real scaling or performance issues. Best practice: fix the root cause, then tune health checks and timeouts as a secondary step. Example: don't change health check path to force a target healthy state; instead correct the service so it answers the intended health endpoint.

content.html:
Common Mistakes
Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
Recognize recurring pitfalls and apply corrective practices that leave systems healthier after the fix.
Security group mismatch: targets must allow LB source; avoid opening wide CIDR ranges unnecessarily.
Wrong health check path/port: ensure the health endpoint returns expected codes and is reachable.
Idle timeout too low: long-running requests may need higher idle timeout to avoid 504s.
DNS caching: stale DNS can point to retired load balancers; validate resolution.
Avoid quick parameter changes as the first response. Gather logs, metrics, and connectivity evidence so your remediation addresses the true root cause, not just the symptom.
Mini checklist
  • Confirm SG and NACL rules before changing health checks.
  • Capture CloudWatch and access logs prior to remediation.
  • Check application resource metrics to rule out overload.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build a repeatable troubleshooting habit for Application and Network Load Balancers. You will learn how to translate symptoms — like 5xx spikes, 503 responses, or slow requests — into focused checks using CloudWatch, access logs, health checks, and network diagnostics. I’ll show concrete signals to watch for, how to validate target group health, and how to rule out common network misconfigurations such as security group mismatches and NACL blocks. We’ll also walk through a short hands-on scenario where a stopped web server causes a “No Healthy Targets” state and a 503 error, and then verify recovery once the service is restored. By the end you’ll have a clear checklist: identify symptoms, confirm health checks, inspect metrics, drill into logs, validate network rules, and test connectivity. This approach reduces guesswork and helps you escalate only when the evidence shows it’s an application, configuration, or infrastructure problem. As you follow the screens, notice how monitoring, logs, and small connectivity tests work together to pinpoint the root cause.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to spot and explain the common symptoms of load balancer problems, use CloudWatch metrics and access logs to pinpoint whether issues originate at the load balancer or backend targets, and resolve health-check failures that stop traffic flow. You will learn to recognize network configuration mistakes—security group mismatches and NACL denies—that quietly block traffic, and you will practice a step-by-step troubleshooting workflow that moves from symptoms to verification. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a real environment. For example, you will identify a 503 spike caused by no healthy targets using both CloudWatch and the target group's health status, and then verify recovery after restarting the service. This set of skills helps reduce downtime and ensures you escalate only when the evidence points to the right layer: LB, network, or application.

This second objectives slide focuses on tool mastery and a troubleshooting sequence. You will learn to map specific CloudWatch metrics to probable causes: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count often signals a load balancer-level problem such as no healthy targets, while HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count points to backend application errors. You will practice using TargetConnectionErrorCount and Latency together to tell whether the problem is connectivity versus slow application responses. You will also use access logs to find per-request evidence like 503 or 504 patterns, timestamps, and client IPs that clarify whether the load balancer or a specific instance triggered the error. Finally, you will apply diagnostic network checks — verify security group rules, confirm NACL allow rules for both inbound and outbound directions, and read VPC Flow Logs to confirm whether traffic is being blocked. Each skill has a measurable milestone so you can demonstrate you can diagnose and validate fixes in a live environment.

The first diagnostic move is to clearly identify the symptom. That means listening to user reports and translating them into measurable signals: are users seeing 5xx server errors, 4xx client errors, 503 service unavailable, 504 timeouts, or simply slow responses? Each class points to a different area. A spike in 5xx codes can mean the load balancer could not reach healthy targets or the targets are returning errors. A dominant Client 4xx pattern usually indicates client-side issues or misrouted requests. A 503 with “No Healthy Targets” is a direct pointer to health check failures. Slow responses and high latency often indicate overloaded targets or network congestion rather than immediate configuration errors. Concrete example: if several users report 503 and CloudWatch shows UnHealthyHostCount increased, you should immediately check the target group's health status and the instance’s service. A common misconception is to restart the load balancer first; instead, verify whether targets are unhealthy and why. Key takeaway: use the symptom to choose the right next tool — metrics, logs, or network checks — so you don’t waste time chasing unlikely causes. Ask yourself: does the data point to the load balancer, the network, or the application?

CloudWatch is the first stop for aggregated signals. For Application Load Balancers the most diagnostic metrics are HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count, HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, HealthyHostCount and UnHealthyHostCount, TargetConnectionErrorCount, Latency, and ClientTLSNegotiationErrorCount for HTTPS listeners. Use these values together instead of reading a single metric in isolation. For example, a large HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count spike paired with UnHealthyHostCount > 0 strongly suggests the ALB is returning errors because it lacks healthy targets. By contrast, if HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count is high but HealthyHostCount is stable, the back end is likely returning 5xx responses and you should inspect application logs. TargetConnectionErrorCount indicates failures establishing connections between ALB and targets and often points to security group or NACL rules or resource exhaustion on the target. Latency helps you distinguish between connectivity errors and slow application responses. A common error is to treat Latency spikes as transient client problems; instead check target C P U, memory, or thread pools. A quick example: you see high TargetConnectionErrorCount and connection resets — verify that the target’s security group permits inbound from the ALB security group and that the instance is responsive on the health-check port. Closing question: which two metrics will you check first when you see a 5xx spike?

Network Load Balancers operate at Layer 4 and provide a different set of signals. Key metrics include HealthyHostCount and UnHealthyHostCount, TargetConnectionErrorCount, TCP_Target_Reset_Count, UDP_Target_Dropped_Count, and ConsumedLCUs. These metrics reveal whether connections are being established and maintained, and whether the targets are dropping or resetting connections. For instance, a growing TCP_Target_Reset_Count often indicates the target is actively refusing or resetting connections — possibly due to the application closing sockets or resource constraints. Similarly, UDP_Target_Dropped_Count points to packet-level loss or unhandled port traffic. ConsumedLCUs helps you understand NLB capacity costs but can also indicate heavy load patterns. A common diagnostic step is to verify that the target’s security group and network ACLs allow the correct IP ranges and ephemeral ports to respond. One misconception is treating NLB behavior like ALB behavior: NLB preserves source IPs and connection errors often manifest differently. Practical check: if TargetConnectionErrorCount increases while HealthyHostCount drops, verify that the instance is listening and that network rules permit the connection and return traffic. How would you confirm whether resets are application-initiated or network-blocked? CloudWatch Metrics for NLBs means nlb metrics focus on connection-level behavior; resets and dropped counts point to target or network-level problems rather than http semantics.. In practical terms, layer 4 signals, connection errors, and consumed lcus. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Access logs provide the per-request detail that aggregated metrics cannot. ALB access logs record client IP, request timestamp, the ALB and target response codes, request processing time, target IP, and X-Forwarded-For headers. NLB access logs capture TCP/UDP connection records including source/destination IPs and ports and connection status. These logs are stored in S3 and are best queried with a service like Amazon Athena. A concrete example: when you see repeated 503 responses from an ALB, query the access logs for elb_status_code and target_status_code to see whether the ALB or the target returned the error and to identify problematic client IPs or request paths. A frequent mistake is to assume access logs are optional; in complex or intermittent issues per-request logs are essential for reproduction and root cause. When using Athena, parse timestamps and filter by load balancer name and target IP to narrow results to a window where a metric spike occurred. Final thought: always correlate access-log evidence with CloudWatch spikes and health-check timestamps to build a convincing chain of cause and effect. Analyzing Access Logs means access logs give the per-request evidence to confirm whether errors are generated by alb, nlb, or targets and to identify offending requests or clients.. In practical terms, using alb and nlb logs to find request-level causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Health check failures are among the most common reasons for routing problems and 503 responses. Use a focused sequence: first, confirm the EC2 instance is running and the application process is listening on the expected port. For HTTP/HTTPS health checks, verify the configured path returns a 200 OK and that any authentication or application-layer redirects are not interfering. Next, confirm security groups allow inbound traffic on the health check port from the load balancer’s security group for ALBs or from the NLB private IPs/VPC CIDR range for NLBs. Check Network ACLs on the target subnet to ensure both inbound and outbound traffic on the health-check and ephemeral ports are allowed; remember NACLs are stateless so you must permit return traffic explicitly. Common application causes include the service being stopped, misconfigured binding addresses, or application logic returning errors. A frequent misconception is to alter health check thresholds before confirming the root cause; prefer fixing the underlying issue, then adjust thresholds if required for expected behavior. Example: if health checks report HTTP 502, inspect application logs to find errors generating the 502, restart the app only after you understand the error, then re-evaluate health checks. This sequence prevents misdiagnosis and unnecessary configuration changes.

A large class of load balancer problems stem from the network path. Start by validating the load balancer’s security group allows inbound traffic on listener ports from the expected client ranges. For ALBs, ensure the target’s security group allows traffic from the ALB’s security group; for NLBs, consider preserved source IPs and allow the appropriate client or VPC CIDR ranges. Check Network ACLs on both the load balancer and target subnets for explicit denies and remember that NACLs are stateless — you must allow both inbound and outbound flows. Confirm routing tables direct traffic correctly for internet-facing versus internal load balancers. If DNS resolution is used, verify the ALB DNS name resolves and that cached or stale DNS entries are not pointing to old resources. When in doubt, enable VPC Flow Logs on the affected subnets to record IP traffic and confirm whether packets are arriving and being dropped. A common misconception is that security groups are stateful enough to ignore NACLs; ignoring NACLs can leave packets dropped silently. Example diagnostic: if VPC Flow Logs show no accept entries from the load balancer to the target, inspect NACLs and routing immediately. The bottom line: verify all layers of the path — listeners, SGs, NACLs, routes, DNS, and flow logs — before concluding the application is at fault.

When the issue is not obvious, follow a reproducible approach: verify symptoms, check health checks, review CloudWatch metrics, examine access logs, inspect network configuration, test connectivity, and finally review application logs. Start by clearly documenting what is failing and when. Then, check target group health — an unhealthy target frequently explains routing failures. Use CloudWatch to find metric anomalies that match the symptom window. Drill into access logs next to see per-request evidence and client patterns. After that, inspect security groups, NACLs, and route tables; enable VPC Flow Logs if you need packet-level confirmation. Perform connectivity checks with curl, telnet, or netcat from an instance in the same VPC, and from the target subnet to confirm reachability. Only after all network checks are clean should you dig into application logs. A common pitfall is interleaving configuration changes without locking in the evidence; always capture metrics and logs before and after changes so you can verify the effect. Example workflow: document 503 occurrence, confirm UnHealthyHostCount, query access logs for 503 timestamps, validate SG/NACLs and routes, run curl to the target health path, then examine application logs. This repeatable method helps you escalate with confidence when you need peer or vendor support.

A common misconception is to wait for too long before checking access logs; immediately capture logs and metrics so you can link timestamps. After you make a change — whether restarting a service, updating an SG, or changing a route — you must verify the fix. Begin by re-running the symptom checks and validating that CloudWatch metrics moved back toward expected levels. Use targeted connectivity tests: curl the health-check path and application endpoints from an EC2 in the same VPC and from the load balancer where possible. For TCP issues use telnet or netcat to confirm the port accepts connections. If you changed security groups, re-check VPC Flow Logs to see that previously dropped packets are now accepted. Observe the target group's health for successful status transitions; remember health checks often require a few intervals to flip state. Also re-query access logs for the same timestamps to confirm the request returned a successful code. A common error is to declare success based solely on the service process appearing 'running' — always confirm that traffic actually flows through the load balancer and the client sees a healthy response. Final question: after a fix, which two data sources will you compare to confirm recovery and why?

Experienced teams often run into a predictable set of mistakes. Security group mismatches are the most frequent cause of 'no healthy targets' or connection errors; ensure the target SG allows inbound from the load balancer source rather than broadly opening ports. Incorrect health check path or port is another common error: verify the configured path returns the expected 200 OK and that the application is actually listening on that port. Idle timeout settings can cause 504 Gateway Timeout errors when backend requests legitimately take longer than the default ALB idle timeout. DNS caching can mislead you into troubleshooting the wrong endpoint; clear caches or validate resolution before changing infrastructure. Target overload and resource exhaustion can masquerade as networking problems; always check application logs and resource metrics. One misconception is to immediately increase timeouts or change thresholds — this may hide real scaling or performance issues. Best practice: fix the root cause, then tune health checks and timeouts as a secondary step. Example: don't change health check path to force a target healthy state; instead correct the service so it answers the intended health endpoint.

These key concepts summarize the chapter: CloudWatch Metrics provide aggregated signals that help you narrow problem domains; Access Logs give per-request evidence needed for root cause analysis; and Target Group Health Checks determine whether traffic is routed to back ends. Keep these as a mental checklist when troubleshooting: metrics to spot anomalies, logs to confirm who and when, and health checks to verify routing. Practice correlating these sources with network checks — security groups, network ACLs, routes, and VPC Flow Logs — to resolve complex connectivity issues quickly. Treat diagnostics as a chain of evidence: each piece should either rule in or rule out a layer of the stack. This way your remediation is targeted, auditable, and reversible if needed.
